buying-campervan-nz.title: How to Buy a Campervan in New Zealand: The Backpacker Guide (2026)
buying-campervan-nz.description: Real prices, a step-by-step inspection routine, WOF, REGO, insurance and self-contained rules — everything you need to buy a campervan in New Zealand without getting burned.

content.intro: So you've just landed in Auckland, everyone at the hostel is talking about buying a van, and you have no idea where to start. Good news: in the next 15 minutes you'll get the full picture — real prices, a proven inspection routine, the scams to dodge, and the exact paperwork. This is the guide we wish we'd had before our first NZ road trip.

items.title: Why buy instead of rent?
items.text: Renting costs $60–150 a day. Buying a $7,000 van for 6 months and selling it for $6,000 costs you about $5 a day plus fuel. That's why almost every long-stay backpacker buys — and with a smart resale, some even break even. The catch: the savings only work if you buy a healthy van. That's what the rest of this guide is for.

items.title: The NZ jargon, decoded
rows: WOF
Warrant of Fitness — the periodic safety inspection every vehicle needs
No valid WOF = you can't legally drive
REGO
Vehicle registration, paid to use public roads
Sold per 3, 6 or 12 months (~$100/year for petrol vans)
RUC
Road User Charges — a per-km tax paid only by diesel vehicles
About $76 per 1,000 km, on top of fuel
Self-contained
Certified with toilet + water tanks (green or blue sticker)
Required for most freedom camping
CarJam
An online vehicle history report
Reveals debts, odometer fraud and stolen vehicles
PPSR
Personal Property Securities Register — the official debt register
A $3 check that stops you inheriting someone's loan

items.title: 📝 Good to know
items.text: You do NOT need to be a NZ resident to buy a vehicle. A passport and a local address (your hostel works) are enough. Most backpackers drive on their home licence or an International Driving Permit — just make sure it's valid in English.

items.title: How long does it take?
items.text: Plan 3 to 7 days in a big city: a couple of days browsing listings, a few viewings, one mechanical inspection, and 15 minutes of paperwork. Rushing it on day one is exactly how people buy lemons.
items.expertTip: Book your first week of accommodation in Auckland or Christchurch — that's where the van supply lives.

items.text: See what's for sale right now across New Zealand

items.title: Price tiers on the backpacker market (NZD)
rows: Under $4,000
Old people-movers (Estima, Serena, Odyssey) with a mattress in the back
High kms, rust, short WOF — inspection is non-negotiable
The classic backpacker vans: Hiace, Bongo, Vanette, L300 — often self-contained
The sweet spot for value; verify the certification is genuine
Younger vans with proper builds: solar, fridge, insulation
Pay for what helps YOU travel, not for fairy lights
High-top vans, 4WD Delicas, small motorhomes
Harder to resell fast at the end of a trip
items.caption: For reference: the average listing on Kiwi Van Market sits around $8,000–10,000.

items.title: ✅ Quick Checklist: the hidden costs first-timers forget
items: Insurance: $300–600/year (third party is the backpacker standard)
Pre-purchase mechanical inspection: $150–180 — the best money you'll spend
Cook Strait ferry with a van: $250–450 return
A $1,000 emergency fund for repairs (battery, tyres, water pump)

items.title: ⚠️ Common Mistake
items.text: Spending every dollar on the van itself. Keep $1,000 aside for surprises — a battery, a tyre, a water pump. A breakdown with an empty account is how road trips end early.

items.title: Can you negotiate? (Yes. Politely.)
items.text: Almost every listed price has 10–15% of room — more at the end of the season, when sellers have a flight to catch. Point at real things: WOF expiry, tyre wear, kilometres, a tired leisure battery. Cash today beats promises tomorrow.
items.expertTip: 💡 Ask when the seller flies out. Three days before departure, an $8,500 van becomes a $7,200 van.

items.title: Petrol or diesel? The honest maths
items.text: Diesel is cheaper at the pump but pays RUC (~$76 per 1,000 km) and services cost more. Petrol is simpler: no RUC, cheaper maintenance, and for a typical 10,000–15,000 km trip the total cost difference is small. Rule of thumb: under 15,000 km, petrol usually wins on simplicity.

sections.title: Where to Buy (and Where to Be Careful)

items.title: Your options, compared honestly
rows: Online marketplaces (like Kiwi Van Market)
Photos, WOF/REGO shown upfront, CarJam history button, direct chat with the owner
Popular vans go fast — check daily
Facebook backpacker groups
Huge volume, real bargains exist
Zero verification, scams, half the posts are already sold
Backpacker car markets
See many vans in one morning
Dealers posing as travellers, entry fees
Dealers
Consumer guarantees, lower risk
20–40% more expensive, few true backpacker vans

items.title: Timing beats everything
items.text: Buy where travellers land: Auckland all year, Christchurch for the South Island. And buy when they leave — February to April floods the market with departing backpackers' vans. October to December is a seller's market: arrive early or pay more.

items.title: ⚠️ The classic scams
items.text: A 'friend overseas' who will ship the van after a deposit. A seller refusing a mechanical inspection. A price way under market with pressure to decide today. A request for a deposit just to 'hold' a van you haven't seen. Any one of these: walk away. There is always another van.

sections.title: The 30-Minute Inspection That Saves You Thousands

items.caption: Always check the oil BEFORE the engine warms up — a cold start tells the truth.

items.title: The mayo test (30 seconds, deal-breaker)
items.text: Open the oil cap. A milky, mayonnaise-like paste under it usually means the head gasket is gone — a $2,000+ repair on a $5,000 van. Close the bonnet, say thank you, and leave.

items.title: Cold start
items.text: Ask the seller NOT to warm up the engine before you arrive. A pre-warmed engine is the oldest trick for hiding rough starts.

items.title: Watch the exhaust
items.text: White or blue smoke at start-up means engine trouble. A puff of steam on a cold morning is fine; a cloud that keeps coming is not.

items.title: Cambelt / timing belt history
items.text: Critical on Hiace and many diesels. Ask when it was last replaced and at what kms — if this belt lets go while driving, it can take the whole engine with it. No proof of replacement on a high-km van? Budget for the job or lower your offer.

items.title: Brakes
items.text: Straight-line stop from 50 km/h: no squealing, no pulling to one side, pedal firm.

items.title: Gearbox
items.text: Test every gear — including reverse. Crunching or hesitation is a repair bill in waiting.

items.title: Steering at speed
items.text: Take it on the motorway. Any wobble at 100 km/h points to alignment, tyres or suspension.

items.title: Rust — the NZ killer
items.text: Wheel arches, window seals, under the carpet, and underneath the van. Surface rust on panels is manageable; rust on structural rails or floor pans is a walk-away.

items.title: Suspension
items.text: Drive over a speed bump slowly and listen for clunks. Push down on each corner — it should settle, not bounce.

items.title: Everything electric
items.text: Windows, lights, wipers, stereo, USB plugs, interior lights. Small failures reveal how the van was cared for.

items.title: Water systems and mould
items.text: Run the taps, check under the sink, lift the mattress. Brown ceiling rings and a damp smell mean water ingress.

items.title: Tyres
items.text: Uneven wear across the tread = alignment or suspension issues. A set of four van tyres costs $600–1,000.

items.title: VIN matches everywhere
items.text: Compare the VIN on the dashboard, the door jamb and the paperwork. Mismatches can mean accident history or a stolen vehicle.

items.title: Then pay a professional — always
items.text: A pre-purchase inspection at VTNZ, AA or any garage costs $150–180. They put the van on a hoist and find what you physically cannot see. A seller who refuses an inspection is telling you everything.
items.expertTip: 🎯 Run the plate through CarJam before you even travel to a viewing — money owing on a van becomes YOUR problem after purchase.

items.text: Get the full 30-point printable buyer checklist

items.title: 📝 Good to know
items.text: On Kiwi Van Market, every listing shows WOF and REGO expiry upfront, and includes a CarJam history button when the seller provides the plate — so you can do the two big checks before you even message anyone.

items.title: The good news
items.text: New Zealand makes vehicle paperwork genuinely easy. No notary, no lawyer, no waiting weeks. Six steps, done the same day, most of them free.

items.title: Run the history checks
items.text: CarJam with the plate number (stolen status, odometer history, WOF record), plus a $3 PPSR check with the VIN — if finance is still owing, the lender can repossess the van from YOU after purchase.

items.title: Verify WOF and REGO
items.text: At least 3 months of WOF left (or freshly passed), and REGO current — not 'on hold'. Both visible on the windscreen and on the listing.

items.title: Write a receipt
items.text: Price, date, both names and passport numbers, plate and VIN, the words 'sold as seen'. Two copies, both signed. It takes five minutes and settles every future argument.

items.title: Transfer ownership TOGETHER
items.text: Both of you complete the change of ownership online at nzta.govt.nz (or at any NZ Post shop) the day you buy. About $9, needs your passport and an address — your hostel is fine.

items.title: Activate insurance before driving off
items.text: Third-party cover takes 20 minutes online and works with a foreign licence. Driving uninsured is gambling your whole trip on one intersection.

items.title: Buy RUC if it's a diesel
items.text: Check the odometer against the RUC distance already purchased. Unpaid RUC becomes your debt. Top up online at nzta.govt.nz in 1,000 km blocks.

items.title: ⚠️ Common Mistake
items.text: Paying now and 'sorting the papers later'. If the seller never files the transfer, their speeding tickets become yours — and legally, the van may not even be yours. Same day, together, no exceptions.
New to WOF, REGO and RUC? Read the plain-English rules guide

sections.title: Self-Contained: Your Ticket to Free Camping

items.caption: The certification sticker: your key to legal freedom camping.

items.title: What the sticker actually means
items.text: A certified self-contained van carries fresh water, a grey-water tank and a toilet. Since the rule change, new certifications (green sticker) require a fixed toilet — older blue-sticker certifications are being phased out as they expire. The certificate belongs to the vehicle and has an expiry date.

items.title: Why it's worth real money
items.text: Without certification, you'll pay $20–50 a night for campsites. With it, thousands of legal freedom camping spots become free. Over 4 months, that's easily $1,500+ saved — and certified vans resell faster, at better prices.

items.title: ⚠️ Common Mistake
items.text: Trusting the words 'self-contained' in an ad. Ask to SEE the certificate and check its expiry — then verify the certification number. A $400 freedom-camping fine ruins a good week.

items.title: Download these two apps tonight
items.text: CamperMate and Rankers show every legal camping spot, dump station and public shower in the country, with reviews from other travellers. They're free, and they're how everyone actually finds where to sleep.

sections.title: Selling It When You Leave (Think About It Now)

items.title: Your exit plan starts at purchase
items.text: The van you buy today is the van you must sell in 6 months, from whichever city you fly out of. Popular models — Hiace, Bongo, L300 — with valid WOF, REGO and self-contained certification sell in days. Rare or tired vans sell in weeks, under pressure, at a loss.

items.title: The seasonal money machine
items.text: Buy in Christchurch in March from a leaving backpacker (low season, low price). Sell in Auckland in November to an arriving one (high season, high price). Travellers who ride this calendar regularly sell for MORE than they paid.

items.title: 📝 Good to know
items.text: Listing your van on Kiwi Van Market is free, with no commission — and you can offer a buy-back deal to make your listing stand out. Put it live 3–4 weeks before your flight, not 3 days.
List your van for free — no commission, direct contact with buyers

items.q: Can foreigners buy a campervan in New Zealand?
items.a: Yes. You don't need residency or a NZ licence: a passport and a local address (your hostel counts) are enough to buy and register a vehicle. Most backpackers drive on their home licence or an International Driving Permit.

items.q: How much should I budget for a backpacker campervan?
items.a: Most travellers spend NZ$5,000–10,000. Solid vans exist under $4,000 but demand a rigorous inspection. The average listing on Kiwi Van Market sits around $8,000–10,000.

items.q: Is car insurance mandatory in New Zealand?
items.a: No — but third-party insurance ($300–600/year) is the backpacker standard. It covers the expensive car you might hit; skipping it is gambling your whole trip on one intersection.
Diesel is cheaper at the pump but pays Road User Charges (about $76 per 1,000 km) and services cost more. If you'll drive under ~15,000 km, petrol usually wins on simplicity.

items.q: What is a WOF and how often do I need it?
items.a: The Warrant of Fitness is New Zealand's periodic safety inspection: every 12 months for vehicles first registered after 2000, every 6 months for older ones. Buy a van with at least 3 months of WOF left.

A $3 search of the Personal Property Securities Register (ppsr.govt.nz) using the VIN. It tells you whether money is still owing on the vehicle — if it is, the lender can repossess the van even after you've paid for it.

items.q: Can I sleep anywhere in my van?
items.a: No. Freedom camping is only legal in permitted areas, and usually only for certified self-contained vehicles. Fines reach $400. CamperMate and Rankers show every legal spot for free.

items.q: What happens if my van breaks down?
items.a: AA Membership (~$99/year) gets you roadside assistance nationwide — most backpackers consider it essential. Keep a $1,000 repair buffer: batteries, tyres and water pumps are the usual suspects on older vans.

items.q: How fast can I sell my van at the end of my trip?
items.a: With a fair price, honest photos and valid paperwork: a few days in high season (October–December), two to four weeks otherwise. List it 3–4 weeks before your flight.

items.q: Where do I check a van's history before buying?
items.a: CarJam, using the plate number: it reveals money owing, stolen status, odometer readings and import history. On Kiwi Van Market, the CarJam button is on the listing whenever the seller provides the plate.

campervan-buyer-checklist.title: Used Campervan Inspection Checklist NZ: How to Check a Van Before Buying
campervan-buyer-checklist.description: A chronological pre-purchase routine for campervans in New Zealand — the homework the night before, the first minutes on site, the walk-around, the test drive, and the handover. Free printable version.

content.intro: Every hostel has the story: someone bought a van on day two, then spent week three paying a mechanic to explain what they missed. You don't avoid becoming that story with luck — you avoid it with a routine. This checklist follows a real viewing in the order it actually happens: the homework the night before, the first minutes on site, the walk-around, the test drive, and the fifteen minutes where money and paperwork change hands. Tick your way through, and by the end you'll know the van better than the seller expects.

sections.title: The Night Before: Homework From the Hostel

items.title: Twenty minutes on your phone, thousands protected
items.text: Most disasters are visible online before you've spent a dollar on gas. Do this from your bunk, the evening before the viewing.

items.title: Plate into CarJam
items.text: The history report shows the ownership count, odometer readings over time, and the WOF pass/fail record. A van that failed its last WOF and went up for sale right after deserves pointed questions.

items.title: VIN into the PPSR
items.text: Three dollars at ppsr.govt.nz tells you whether a lender still has a claim on the vehicle. Finance debt travels with the van — not with the seller.

items.title: Sanity-check the price
items.text: Line the van up against comparable listings: same model, similar year, kms and certification. A price sitting far under the market is a question to answer, not a win to grab.

items.title: Send two messages
items.text: 'Could you send photos of the service records?' and 'Please don't start the engine before I arrive.' The answers — and the tone of them — tell you plenty before you've even met.

items.title: Book daylight and dry weather
items.text: Rain flatters paint and hides oil spots on the driveway. A morning slot also makes a genuine cold start much more likely.
Print the pocket version of this checklist (free, nothing to sign up for)

items.title: Before you touch anything, stand back
items.text: Vans talk, if you give them a few metres of distance and thirty seconds of silence.

items.title: Look at how it sits
items.text: A van leaning toward one corner is telling you about tired springs or suspension before you've opened a door.

items.title: Compare the four tyres
items.text: Four different brands, or fresh fronts over bald rears, describe a van that gets maintained one emergency at a time.

items.title: Open the door and breathe in
items.text: Damp has a smell you can't unsmell. Mould behind wall panels announces itself here first — before your nose adjusts to it.

items.title: Ask how long they've owned it
items.text: Casually. Later, match the answer against the CarJam ownership dates. Honest sellers tell consistent stories without trying.

items.caption: Bring a torch. The van's real history is written underneath it.

items.title: Panel gaps and paint tone
items.text: Uneven gaps between panels, or one door in a slightly different shade, point to accident repairs that nobody volunteered.

items.title: The fridge-magnet trick
items.text: Wrap a magnet in a tea towel and glide it along the sills and wheel arches. Where it stops sticking, someone has smoothed body filler over rust.

items.title: Get underneath with your torch
items.text: Chassis rails, floor pans, sills. Flaking brown crust on anything structural is a walk-away; a light surface bloom on flat panels is a negotiation.

items.title: Window rubbers and roof seams
items.text: NZ vans live outside, often near salt air. Paint bubbling around the glass is rust working from the inside out — the expensive direction.

items.title: Lift whatever lifts
items.text: Carpet corners, floor mats, the boot liner. Floors rot quietly in the dark, and a two-second peek costs nothing.

sections.title: Bonnet Up, Then the Test Drive

items.title: Confirm the cold start is cold
items.text: Touch the bonnet before anyone turns a key — it should be stone cold. Long cranking, a lumpy idle, or smoke that keeps coming are engine conversations, not details.

items.title: Cap, dipstick, coolant
items.text: Creamy residue under the oil cap points to head-gasket trouble — on an old van, that repair often costs more than the van is worth. Oil should be dark but clean; coolant its proper colour and never oily.

items.title: Ask the cambelt question
items.text: On high-km Japanese vans, ask when the timing belt was last replaced and get it in writing if possible. If that belt lets go mid-trip, it can wreck the engine — no receipt means you price the job into your offer.

items.title: Drive it like New Zealand drives
items.text: Motorway up to 100 km/h (no shake through the wheel), a real hill if you can find one (temperature needle steady, power holding), a slow speed bump (no clunks), and one firm, straight brake.

items.title: Radio off, window half down
items.text: You're listening for whines, knocks and grinding — a soundtrack is the cheapest way to hide all three.

items.title: Every gear, twice
items.text: Reverse included. Hesitation or crunching between shifts is gearbox money you'd be volunteering to spend.

items.title: 📝 Good to know
items.text: Above roughly $5,000, a professional pre-purchase inspection ($150–180 at a garage, AA or VTNZ) buys you a hoist, trained eyes and a written report you can negotiate with. Cheap insurance on a big decision.

sections.title: The Camper Kit: Test, Don't Admire

items.title: A pretty build sells vans; a working build keeps trips alive
items.text: Fairy lights are lovely. Water pressure, cold beer and charged phones are lovelier. Test the systems like you already live in it.

items.title: Certificate in hand, not in the ad
items.text: For self-containment, see the actual document: expiry date, and that it matches THIS vehicle. Adverts say 'self-contained'; only certificates prove it.

items.title: Water in, water out
items.text: Run the tap, watch the drain flow, then open the cupboard under the sink and press the wood. Soft timber remembers every past leak.

items.title: Plug your phone into every socket
items.text: The fastest audit of a 12V system ever invented. Bring your own cable.

items.title: Run the fridge and lights on the battery
items.text: Engine off, ten minutes. A healthy leisure battery shrugs this off; a dying one sags visibly. Ask its age — past three or four years, budget for a replacement.

items.title: Make 'it has solar' mean something
items.text: Ask for the panel wattage and the controller brand. Without numbers, 'solar' can mean a trickle charger and an optimistic sticker.

items.title: Sniff the gas locker
items.text: Any gas smell — or a cooker with no compliance certificate — is a safety problem before it's a paperwork one.

items.title: Lift the mattress
items.text: Brown rings on the plywood underneath are the honest autobiography of every roof leak the van has ever had.

sections.title: Money and Paperwork: The Last Fifteen Minutes

items.title: Re-read the two windscreen labels
items.text: WOF and REGO: both current, and ideally months from expiry. Anything about to lapse is a cost you're inheriting — say so, politely, with a number.

items.title: Diesel? Read the RUC label
items.text: The distance purchased should cover the odometer reading. Any shortfall becomes your bill at the NZTA counter.

items.title: Write the receipt before money moves
items.text: Price, date, both names and passport numbers, plate, VIN, the words 'sold as seen'. Two copies, both signed. Five minutes that settle every future argument.

items.title: Transfer ownership together, on the spot
items.text: Ten minutes online at nzta.govt.nz, about $9, done side by side. 'We'll sort it tomorrow' is how travellers end up owning a stranger's speeding tickets — or not owning the van at all.

items.title: Insure it before you turn the key
items.text: Third-party cover takes twenty minutes online and accepts foreign licences. The drive back to the hostel is already a drive.

items.title: None of these are negotiation openers
items.text: They're exits. The NZ van market always has another one for sale — this week, at a fair price, from someone straightforward.

items.title: 🚩 If you meet one of these, leave
items: You're not allowed to arrange an independent inspection — whatever the excuse
The timeline is doing the selling ('two other buyers are coming at four')
The seller's story doesn't line up with the CarJam ownership dates
'My mechanic mate already checked it' is offered instead of documents
A special discount appears only if you pay cash today
The VINs on the windscreen, door pillar and papers don't all match

items.title: 📝 Good to know
items.text: On Kiwi Van Market, WOF, REGO and self-contained status sit on every listing, with a CarJam button when the plate is provided — the boring checks are done from your bunk, before you've spent a dollar on gas.
Browse campervans with the paperwork visible upfront

items.q: Should I bring someone to a van viewing?
items.a: If you can, yes. A second person watches the seller's reactions while you watch the van — and pressure tactics deflate fast in front of an audience. Solo? Phone a friend during the viewing and think out loud.

items.q: Is a cheap OBD2 scanner worth buying?
items.a: For about $30, absolutely. Plugged in under the dash, it reads stored engine fault codes in minutes and catches the classic trick of clearing a warning light the morning of a sale. It doesn't replace a mechanic — it decides whether you need one.

items.q: How long should I allow for a proper viewing?
items.a: Ninety minutes minimum: fifteen standing back and walking around, thirty on systems and paperwork, thirty on the road, and buffer to think without pressure. Anyone rushing you through it is answering a question you didn't ask.

items.q: Is it normal to leave a deposit?
items.a: Only after an inspection you're satisfied with, only with a written receipt stating the amount and the conditions, and never to 'reserve' a van you haven't seen in person. For the balance, an in-person bank transfer beats cash — it writes its own receipt.

wof-rego-ruc-insurance-nz.title: WOF, REGO, RUC & Insurance in New Zealand: Van Rules Explained Simply
wof-rego-ruc-insurance-nz.description: The four vehicle rules every campervan traveller must understand in NZ — what they cost, when they're due, and the fines if you get them wrong. In plain English.

content.intro: Four acronyms rule your van life in New Zealand: WOF, REGO, RUC and (unofficially) ACC. Get them right and you'll never think about them again. Get them wrong and you're looking at fines, a van you can't legally drive, or debts you inherited from the previous owner. Here's each one, in plain English, with real numbers.

items.title: What it is
items.text: The WOF is New Zealand's periodic vehicle safety inspection. It checks brakes, tyres, lights, steering, seatbelts, rust and more. Without a current WOF, you cannot legally drive — and your insurance can refuse to pay out.

items.title: How often is a WOF due?
rows: First registered after 1 January 2000
Every 12 months
First registered before 2000 (most cheap backpacker vans!)
Every 6 months
Brand new vehicles
First WOF at 3 years
items.caption: A test costs $60–80 at VTNZ, AA or most garages, and takes about 45 minutes.

items.title: What if it fails?
items.text: You get a list of what to fix, and you can't legally drive except to get repairs and re-test. Most places offer a free or cheap re-check within 28 days. This is why a van with a nearly-expired WOF is worth less: you're inheriting the gamble.
items.expertTip: 💡 Buying? A fresh WOF from VTNZ or AA carries more weight than one from an unknown garage — and 3+ months remaining should be your minimum.

items.title: What it is
items.text: REGO is the licence fee to use public roads, shown by the label on your windscreen. You buy it in 3, 6 or 12-month blocks, online at nzta.govt.nz or at NZ Post — it takes five minutes.

items.title: What REGO costs (typical van)
rows: Petrol van or car
Diesel van
Less for REGO itself — but you pay RUC on top (next section)

items.title: ⚠️ When buying a van
items.text: Check the REGO isn't 'on hold' (a seller can suspend it to save money while selling). Reactivating is easy but it's YOUR cost, and driving while it's on hold is a $200 fine.

items.title: What it is
items.text: Petrol vehicles pay road tax at the pump. Diesel vehicles pay it separately: Road User Charges, bought in 1,000 km blocks (about $76 each) online at nzta.govt.nz. Your windscreen label shows the odometer reading you've paid up to.

items.title: The maths for a typical trip
items.text: A 10,000 km South-plus-North Island loop in a diesel van costs about $760 in RUC on top of fuel. Diesel is cheaper per litre, so on long trips it can still win — but for most backpacker itineraries under 15,000 km, petrol's simplicity is worth more than diesel's savings.

items.title: ⚠️ The trap that catches buyers
items.text: Unpaid RUC follows the VEHICLE, not the seller. Before buying any diesel van, compare the odometer with the RUC distance purchased — the difference is a debt you're about to inherit.

items.title: The surprise: insurance is not legally required
items.text: New Zealand doesn't mandate car insurance. But before you celebrate: if you cause a crash uninsured, you personally owe the damage — and hitting a $80,000 ute is a real possibility. That's why virtually every traveller carries at least third-party cover.

items.title: Your three options
rows: Third party
Other people's vehicles and property (not your van)
Third party, fire & theft
The above + your van if stolen or burned
Comprehensive
Everything, including your own crash damage
$700+ — rarely worth it on a $6,000 van
items.caption: Foreign licences are accepted by mainstream NZ insurers; you can sign up online with a passport and a NZ address.

items.title: And ACC?
items.text: New Zealand's Accident Compensation Corporation covers INJURY treatment for everyone in NZ — including tourists — regardless of fault. It's real and it's free. But it covers people, not property: your medical bills after a crash, yes; your van or the other car, no. ACC is why travel insurance and vehicle insurance still matter.

items.title: What it costs to get it wrong
items: Driving without a current WOF: $200 fine — and your insurance can refuse claims
Unpaid RUC: assessed against the vehicle, plus penalties
Freedom camping without certification (where required): up to $400
No insurance: no fine — but one at-fault crash can cost you tens of thousands

items.text: Ready to buy? Read the full step-by-step buying guide
Going to an inspection? Take the 30-point checklist

items.q: Can I drive a van with an expired WOF?
items.a: Only directly to a testing station or to a garage for booked repairs. Anywhere else risks a $200 fine — and voids most insurance policies.

items.q: What does 'REGO on hold' mean when buying a van?
items.a: The seller suspended the registration to save money. The van can't legally be driven until it's reactivated (easy, online, but at your cost) — and it may need a new WOF first.

items.q: How do I buy RUC for a diesel van?
items.a: Online at nzta.govt.nz or at NZ Post, in blocks of 1,000 km (~$76). Buy enough to cover your planned distance; unused RUC can be refunded when you sell.

items.q: Can foreigners get NZ vehicle insurance?
items.a: Yes — mainstream insurers cover drivers on foreign licences or International Driving Permits. You sign up online in about 20 minutes with a passport and a NZ address (your hostel works).
No. ACC covers accident injuries in NZ for everyone, but not illness, not your belongings, not your van, and not liability. Keep your travel insurance, and put third-party cover on the van.

freedom-camping-nz.title: Freedom Camping in New Zealand - Rules & Best Spots 2025
freedom-camping-nz.description: Complete guide to freedom camping in New Zealand. Where you can camp for free, self-contained requirements, fines to avoid, and the best freedom camping spots.

content.intro: Freedom camping is one of the best ways to experience New Zealand's stunning nature without breaking the bank. But there are rules you need to follow to camp legally and protect the environment.

items.title: Self-Contained Required
items.text: Most freedom camping spots require a certified self-contained vehicle. This means having a toilet, fresh water tank, and grey water tank.

items.title: Check Local Rules
items.text: Each council has different rules. Use the CamperMate or WikiCamps app to find legal spots and current restrictions.

items.title: Maximum Stay
items.text: Most spots allow 1-2 nights maximum. Always move on and don't overstay.

items.title: Leave No Trace
items.text: Take all rubbish with you, don't dump grey water on the ground, use proper dump stations.

items.title: Camping in Prohibited Areas
items.text: $200 instant fine. Can be up to $10,000 for repeat offenders or environmental damage.

items.title: Fake Self-Contained Sticker
items.text: $200+ fine. Officers do check - your van must actually have the required facilities.

items.title: Dumping Waste
items.text: Up to $10,000 fine for dumping toilet waste or grey water illegally.

items.title: South Island West Coast
items.text: Most relaxed rules, stunning beaches and forests. Great spots near Hokitika and Greymouth.

items.title: Otago/Southland
items.text: Beautiful lakes and mountains. Many DOC campsites with basic facilities.

items.title: East Cape (North Island)
items.text: Off the beaten track, friendly locals, beautiful coastline.

warnings: Queenstown and popular tourist areas have strict no-camping rules
Auckland city has very limited freedom camping options
Summer (Dec-Feb) is busiest - spots fill up early
Always have a backup plan (paid campsite) in case spots are full

cta.title: Get a Self-Contained Van
cta.text: Freedom camping is only possible with a certified self-contained vehicle. Find one on Kiwi Van Market.

selling-campervan-nz.title: How to Sell Your Campervan in New Zealand - Quick Sale Guide
selling-campervan-nz.description: Sell your campervan fast in New Zealand. Tips for pricing, photos, descriptions, and reaching backpacker buyers. Free listings on Kiwi Van Market.

content.intro: Selling your campervan at the end of your New Zealand adventure doesn't have to be stressful. With the right approach, you can sell quickly and get a fair price.

items.title: Deep Clean
items.text: First impressions matter. Clean inside and out, remove personal items, make it smell fresh.

items.title: Minor Repairs
items.text: Fix small issues - they're cheap but make buyers nervous. Worn wiper blades, broken lights, etc.

items.title: Get Fresh WOF
items.text: A van with 6+ months WOF sells faster and for more money. Worth the $50-100 investment.

items.title: Gather Documents
items.text: Have ownership papers, service history, and self-contained certificate ready to show.

items.title: Timing
items.text: Shoot during golden hour (early morning or late afternoon) for best lighting.

items.title: Angles
items.text: Include: front 3/4 view, rear, both sides, interior bed setup, kitchen area, dashboard, engine bay.

items.title: Quantity
items.text: 10-15 photos is ideal. More photos = more trust = faster sale.

items.title: Honesty
items.text: Include photos of any damage or wear. Buyers appreciate honesty and it saves time.

items.title: Research Market
items.text: Check similar vans on TradeMe and Kiwi Van Market. Price competitively.

items.title: Be Realistic
items.text: End of season (March-April) prices drop. Factor in your timeline.

items.title: Room to Negotiate
items.text: List 5-10% above your minimum. Kiwi buyers expect to negotiate.

items.title: Kiwi Van Market
items.text: Free listings, backpacker-focused audience. List here first!

items.title: Facebook Groups
items.text: Backpackers NZ groups have active buy/sell sections. Good for quick sales.

items.title: Hostel Noticeboards
items.text: Physical flyers at backpacker hostels in main cities.

warnings: Beware of scammers asking to pay by unusual methods
Never hand over keys before payment clears
Meet buyers in safe, public places
Complete the ownership transfer properly through NZTA

cta.text: Reach thousands of backpackers looking for campervans. It takes just 5 minutes.

how-to-inspect-campervan-nz.title: Expert Campervan Inspection - The Ultimate NZ Checklist
how-to-inspect-campervan-nz.description: Don't buy a lemon! Our expert guide covers everything from engine health and structural rust to living system checks. Inspect like a pro before you buy.

content.intro: Buying a campervan is your biggest investment in NZ. A "pretty" interior often hides mechanical nightmares. This guide gives you the technical tools to look past the fairy lights and inspect the heart of the vehicle. If a seller rushes you or refuses these checks, walk away immediately.

items.title: The Cold Start Test
items.text: Touch the engine block before starting. If it's warm, the seller might be hiding a difficult start or smoke issues. Start it yourself and watch the exhaust for blue (oil) or white (coolant) smoke.

items.title: The "Mayonnaise" Check
items.text: Open the oil filler cap. A milky, white/beige sludge ("mayo") indicates a blown head gasket - a catastrophic and expensive failure. Avoid at all costs.

items.title: Belts & Cam-belt
items.text: Ask when the cam-belt (timing belt) was last changed. If it snaps, the engine is destroyed. It usually needs changing every 100,000km.

items.title: Chassis & Sills
items.text: Get on the ground with a torch. Look for flaky, bubbling metal on the underside. Surface rust is okay; structural rust (holes or deep flakes) will fail the WOF and ruin the van's value.

items.title: Tyre Wear Patterns
items.text: If tyres are worn more on one side, the wheel alignment is off or suspension components are bent. Budget $500+ for suspension repairs.

items.title: Gearbox & Clutch
items.text: Shift through all gears. If it's a manual, check for a "slipping clutch" by putting it in 4th gear at low speed and flooring the gas - the RPM shouldn't jump without speed.

items.title: Braking & Steering
items.text: Let go of the wheel briefly on a flat road - the van should go straight. Brake hard once (safely) to check for shuddering (warped discs) or pulling to one side.

items.title: The Leak Test
items.text: Look for dark stains around windows and skylights. Press your thumb into the walls - if they feel soft/spongy, there is wood rot from water ingress.

items.title: Deep Cycle Battery
items.text: Test the voltage of the leisure battery with a multimeter if possible. Turn on all lights and the fridge to see if the voltage drops instantly.

warnings: NEVER buy a van without a pre-purchase inspection from an independent mechanic ($140-180)
Check the VIN on CarJam.co.nz to ensure there is no money owing (debt) on the vehicle
Verify the Self-Containment blue card matches the van's plate and is current

cta.text: Compare it with other listings to ensure you're getting a fair price for the condition.

winter-camping-nz.title: Survival Guide: Winter Camping in New Zealand 2025
winter-camping-nz.description: Can you camp in NZ during winter? Yes! Discover the best heated vans, snow-safe roads, and essential gear to stay warm while exploring the Southern Alps.

content.intro: Winter in New Zealand (June to August) transforms the landscape into a snowy wonderland. While many backpackers leave, the smart ones stay for cheaper van prices and empty campsites. But winter camping requires serious preparation. Here is how to survive and thrive in a van when the mercury drops below zero.

items.title: Insulation is Key
items.text: Look for vans with sheep wool or foam insulation. Avoid "bare metal" vans which act like refrigerators at night.

items.title: Diesel Heaters
items.text: The gold standard for winter vanlife. A 2KW diesel heater uses very little fuel and keeps the interior at a cozy 20°C even in a blizzard.

items.title: Certified Self-Contained
items.text: In winter, you'll want to use your own indoor facilities rather than trekking through snow to a campsite toilet.

items.title: -5°C Sleeping Bags
items.text: A standard summer bag won't cut it. Invest in a down sleeping bag or high-tog duvet.

items.title: Snow Chains
items.text: Mandatory on many South Island passes (Crown Range, Milford Road). Practice putting them on before you actually need them!

items.title: Dehumidifiers
items.text: Condensation is your enemy. Use passive moisture absorbers to prevent mould from growing on your mattress.

items.title: Ohakune (North Island)
items.text: The gateway to Mt Ruapehu. Great vibes and many vans with heaters for sale here.

items.title: Wanaka & Queenstown
items.text: The heart of NZ winter. Expect professional ski setups and plenty of long-term van parking.

items.title: Tekapo
items.text: Coldest place in NZ but the best stargazing. Make sure your batteries are fully charged!

warnings: Black ice is a major hazard - drive late in the morning when the sun has melted it
Avoid high alpine passes during heavy snow warnings unless you are an experienced driver
Always check the MetService app for weather alerts before moving locations

cta.title: Need a Van with a Heater?
cta.text: Filter our listings to find fully insulated vans with diesel heaters.

south-island-road-trip.title: The Ultimate 14-Day South Island Road Trip Itinerary
south-island-road-trip.description: The most iconic road trip in the world. From Christchurch to Milford Sound, discover the best hidden campsites and photo spots for your van adventure.

content.intro: The South Island of New Zealand is the ultimate playground for campervans. This 14-day loop takes you through turquoise lakes, ancient glaciers, and dramatic fiords. Pack your camera and get ready for the trip of a lifetime.

items.title: Day 1-3: Lake Tekapo & Pukaki
items.text: Star gazing and hiking at Mt Cook. Camp at Lake Pukaki (freedom camping available for SC vans).

items.title: Day 4-5: Wanaka
items.text: The famous "That Wanaka Tree" and Roy's Peak hike for the best views in the country.

items.title: Day 6-7: Queenstown
items.text: Adventure capital. Great for a luxury campsite night with a hot shower and laundry.

items.title: Day 8-9: Milford Sound
items.text: Cruising the fiords. Note: There is no phone signal here, so download your maps offline.

items.title: Day 10-12: West Coast
items.text: Fox Glacier, Franz Josef, and the Pancake Rocks. Stunning coastal driving.

items.title: Day 13-14: Arthur's Pass
items.text: Drive back to Christchurch through the heart of the Southern Alps.

warnings: Sandflies on the West Coast are brutal - buy "Goodbye Sandfly" repellent locally
Always book Milford Sound cruises in advance as they sell out daily
Fuel is expensive in small towns - fill up in main cities like Christchurch or Queenstown

cta.title: Start Your Journey
cta.text: Pick up your campervan in Christchurch and hit the road today.

best-vanlife-apps-nz.title: 6 Essential Apps for Every NZ Vanlife Traveller (2025)
best-vanlife-apps-nz.description: Don't leave without these! From finding secret campsites to saving money on fuel, these apps will save you time and hundreds of dollars.

content.intro: In 2025, your phone is just as important as your van's spare tyre. These 6 apps are the difference between an average trip and an epic adventure in New Zealand.

items.title: CamperMate (Free)
items.text: The #1 app. Shows freedom camping spots, paid parks, public toilets, and petrol stations.

items.title: WikiCamps NZ
items.text: Great for finding hidden gems that CamperMate might miss. One-time small fee but worth it.

items.title: Gaspy
items.text: The community-driven fuel price app. Save 10-20 cents per litre by driving 2 mins further.

items.title: Kiwi Van Market
items.text: Bookmark our site for current resale values and to find parts/repairs across the country.

items.title: MetService
items.text: Essential for mountain weather and road closures.

items.title: NZTA Waka Kotahi
items.text: Real-time road hazard alerts. Critical for South Island travel.

warnings: Always download the "South Island" and "North Island" offline maps in Google Maps
Don't trust GPS times - NZ roads are windy and often take 30% longer than expected

cta.text: Set up your van with a 12V charger to keep your phone alive throughout the journey.

top-10-best-vans-nz.title: Top 10 Best Campervans to Buy in New Zealand (2025 Ranking)
top-10-best-vans-nz.description: The definitive ranking of the 10 best campervans for backpackers in New Zealand. Prices, reliability, resale value and expert tips for each model.

content.intro: Choosing the right campervan is the single most important decision of your New Zealand trip. The wrong van means breakdowns on remote roads, failed WOFs, and a stressful sale at the end. This ranking is based on real market data, mechanic feedback, and thousands of backpacker experiences.

items.title: 1. Toyota Hiace (1990–2005)
items.text: The undisputed king. 70% of NZ rental fleets use the Hiace for a reason: it is near-indestructible. Parts are available everywhere, even in tiny West Coast towns. The 2.8L diesel (3L) is the sweet spot between power and economy. Expect to pay NZ$8,000–$18,000 depending on conversion quality.
items.expertTip: The 1KZ-TE engine is legendary but watch for head gasket issues on high-mileage units. The later 1TR petrol engine is bulletproof but thirstier.

items.title: 2. Toyota HiAce (2005–2018 "200 Series")
items.text: The modern evolution. More comfortable, better fuel economy, and a smoother ride. Harder to find as campervans but worth the premium. Budget NZ$15,000–$30,000.
items.expertTip: The 2KD-FTV diesel engine is one of the most reliable engines ever made. If you find one with under 250,000km, buy it.

items.title: 3. Nissan Caravan (E25)
items.text: The budget king. Offers nearly the same space as a Hiace but typically $2,000–$4,000 cheaper. The ZD30 diesel engine is solid. Great option for couples on a tight budget. NZ$6,000–$14,000.
items.expertTip: Check for timing chain rattle on cold start. A noisy chain is a $1,500 repair but not terminal.

items.title: 4. Nissan Elgrand (E51)
items.text: Known as the "King of Vans" — and for good reason. Superior comfort, powerful V6, and a luxury interior. Popular for premium conversions. Not the most fuel-efficient but the driving experience is unmatched. NZ$8,000–$16,000.

items.title: 5. Mitsubishi Delica (L400/D5)
items.text: The only true 4WD van on this list. If you want to explore gravel roads, ski fields, and remote DOC tracks, the Delica is your only option. Compact but incredibly capable. NZ$7,000–$15,000.
items.expertTip: The L400 with the 2.8L diesel is a workhorse. The newer D5 is more refined but rarer and pricier.

items.title: 6. Toyota Estima (Previa)
items.text: A hidden gem for solo travellers or couples. Mid-engine layout means a flat floor for sleeping. Surprisingly spacious. Very fuel-efficient. The best "stealth" camper. NZ$4,000–$10,000.

items.title: 7. Mazda Bongo Friendee
items.text: Compact, quirky, and loveable. The pop-top roof models are perfect for standing up inside. Great fuel economy and easy to park in cities. NZ$5,000–$12,000.

items.title: 8. Ford Transit (2000–2012)
items.text: European reliability in a big body. Lots of interior space for tall conversions. Cheaper to buy but parts can be slightly harder to source than Japanese vans. NZ$5,000–$12,000.

items.title: 9. Toyota TownAce / LiteAce
items.text: The perfect "mini campervan" for solo backpackers. Tiny, fuel-sipping, and surprisingly comfortable for one person. Easy to drive and park anywhere. NZ$3,000–$8,000.

items.title: 10. Mitsubishi L300 Express
items.text: Raw, basic, and cheap. A no-frills option that gets the job done for short 2-3 month trips. Don't expect luxury but it won't break the bank. NZ$2,500–$6,000.
items.expertTip: Great for the "buy cheap, sell cheap" strategy. Perfect if you're only in NZ for a few months.

items.title: Seasonality Matters
items.text: Buy in March-April (end of season) for the best prices. Sell in October-November for maximum return. The difference can be $2,000–$4,000 on the same van.

items.title: Always Get a Pre-Purchase Inspection
items.text: For $150, a mechanic will find issues worth thousands. Never skip this step, especially on diesel engines.

items.title: Check CarJam
items.text: Enter the license plate on CarJam.co.nz to check for money owing, stolen status, odometer rollback, and import history. It's free for basic checks.

warnings: Avoid any van where the seller refuses a mechanical inspection
Japanese imports with under 100,000km on the clock can be suspicious — odometer fraud exists
A "beautiful" interior conversion means nothing if the engine is dying
Budget $1,000–$2,000 on top of purchase price for WOF repairs, registration, and insurance
